articles.body: Containers Europe Gas SFL adds $365m newbuild trio with $333m in charter cover Adis Ajdin October 29, 2026 0 0 1 minute read SFL SFL John Fredriksen-backed SFL Corporation has agreed to acquire three newbuildings for around $365m, securing long-term employment that will add at least $333m to its charter backlog. The New York-listed shipowner said the latest investment covers two 8,800 teu containerships scheduled for delivery in 2027 and a 93,000 cu m dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) due in 2028. The two containerships have been fixed to an unnamed major liner operator on minimum eight-year charters, with extension options for another four years. The agreements also include purchase options at the end of years eight, 10 and 12, together with profit-sharing arrangements. The VLAC will enter a minimum five-year charter with a major commodities group, with options to extend employment by another two years. The charterer will also have the option to initiate a vessel sale during the final two years of the firm period, subject to profit sharing. SFL has not identified the charterers, vessel sellers or shipyards involved. The latest agreements take the company’s additions to fixed-rate charter backlog this year to more than $1.6bn. The investment follows SFL’s move into the VLAC segment earlier this month, when it ordered two 93,000 cu m dual-fuel vessels for about $216m, securing long-term charters with a European investment-grade oil major worth at least $162m. The company has also been recycling capital from older tankers. In early October, SFL agreed to sell four LR2 product tankers and three suezmaxes to commodities trader Trafigura, a transaction expected to generate approximately $275m in net cash proceeds and a $175m book gain. The seven vessels were acquired in 2021, with the disposals marking another stage in SFL’s shift towards contracted shipping assets. SFL has also extended its containership exposure through longer fixtures. In September, the company secured $750m in additional contracted revenue by renewing charters on six 15,400 teu vessels with Hapag-Lloyd for seven years, keeping the ships employed through 2035 and 2036. articles.title: Samudera reports stable container volumes and higher revenue per TEU
articles.summary: Samudera Shipping Line handled 503,000 TEU during the third quarter of 2026, unchanged from the corresponding period last year. articles.body: Samudera Shipping Line handled 503,000 TEU during the third quarter of 2026, unchanged from the corresponding period last year. According to the company’s latest business update, average container shipping revenue increased to US$297 per TEU. This compares with US$252 per TEU in the third quarter of 2025. Samudera said average freight rates were higher year on year. However, bunker and charter hire expenses remained elevated during the quarter. Tanker activity declines Samudera’s bulk and tanker fleet comprised seven vessels during the quarter, down from eight vessels a year earlier. The fleet included three chemical tankers and four gas tankers. Employment days fell from 671 in the third quarter of 2025 to 414 in the same period of 2026. The company attributed the decline to service disruptions in the Middle East, vessel downtime and scheduled drydockings. These factors affected both revenue and operating margins. Samudera also noted that it sold two chemical tankers in June 2026. One vessel was delivered during the second quarter, while the other was delivered in the third quarter. Logistics volumes increase The company’s logistics business recorded higher storage occupancy and cargo-handling volumes. Storage occupancy increased from 173,100 pallet positions in the third quarter of 2025 to 188,900 positions in the latest quarter. Meanwhile, the volume handled rose from 627,500 pallet equivalents to 977,100 pallet equivalents. Samudera attributed the increase to stronger fourth-party logistics activity in Indonesia. However, the logistics segment’s operating margin declined following the rationalisation of the company’s warehouse business in Malaysia.

articles.body: Asia Containers Greater China Korean carrier Namsung returns to China for larger boxships Adis Ajdin October 29, 2026 0 41 1 minute read Namsung Namsung South Korea’s Namsung Shipping has been linked to another containership order in China, with brokers reporting a deal for two firm 7,100 teu vessels at Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation (DSIC), plus options for another pair. Shipbroking sources said the CSSC-owned yard had secured the contract, with deliveries expected between 2030 and 2031. No price or propulsion specifications have been disclosed. The reported agreement would mark Namsung’s first order at DSIC and its second shipbuilding deal in China this year. The Seoul-based carrier entered the Chinese newbuilding market in March, booking two 4,300 teu containerships at CSSC’s Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding. The order formed part of a wider four-vessel agreement also involving fellow South Korean operator Dongyoung Shipping, which contracted two 1,900 teu feeders. Namsung’s latest reported 7,100 teu contract represents a significant increase in vessel size from that earlier order. The carrier, established in 1953, operates primarily across intra-Asian liner trades linking South Korea, Japan, China and Southeast Asia. Its current company website identifies 20 operating vessels, with its network extending across multiple regional services. DSIC has meanwhile built up a substantial commercial orderbook across crude and product tankers, shuttle tankers, bulk carriers and containerships. articles.body: Vard Launches New Energy Construction Vessel for Norwegian Owner Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 (Credit: Vard/LinkedIn) Shipbuilder Vard has launched a new energy construction vessel (ECV) being built for Wind Energy Construction, a Norwegian company partly owned by the founders and owners of Norwind Offshore, with delivery scheduled for the second quarter of 2027. The vessel, designated NB985, was successfully launched on October 27 and is under construction at Vard Vung Tau in Vietnam, Vard announced. Based on Vard's VARD 3 11 design, the vessel is intended for offshore wind and subsea operations, including inspection, maintenance and repair of subsea pipelines, as well as the construction and installation of offshore infrastructure. Measuring 111.5 meters in length and 22.4 meters in beam, the ECV will feature a 3D electric-controlled motion-compensated walk-to-work gangway, a 150-tonne heave-compensated subsea crane and accommodation for up to 120 people. (Credit: Vard/LinkedIn) Vard is responsible for the vessel's design, hull, construction, outfitting and commissioning through its integrated value chain. The shipbuilding contract was signed in 2024 and included an option for an additional vessel. The newbuild also marked the first construction vessel Vard would build with a permanently installed motion-compensated walk-to-work gangway, expanding its capabilities for offshore construction and renewable energy operations. articles.title: US tightens entry rules for ships calling at Somali ports
articles.summary: The US Coast Guard has imposed additional security conditions on commercial vessels arriving in American waters after calling at Somali ports, adding the East African country to its list of jurisdictions considered to have inadequate port security measures. articles.body: Americas Asia Operations Ports and Logistics Regulatory US tightens entry rules for ships calling at Somali ports Adis Ajdin October 29, 2026 0 66 1 minute read Mogadishu Port Mogadishu Port The US Coast Guard has imposed additional security conditions on commercial vessels arriving in American waters after calling at Somali ports, adding the East African country to its list of jurisdictions considered to have inadequate port security measures. The restrictions took effect this week, following a determination that Somalia was not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures at its ports. The decision, published in the US Federal Register, brings the number of countries on the Coast Guard’s affected-port list to 24. Under the established Port Security Advisory framework, ships that have visited an affected country among their previous five port calls face additional security and documentation requirements before entering the US. These include enhanced access controls, security records and reporting to the relevant Coast Guard captain of the port. Vessels may also be inspected for compliance, with deficiencies potentially resulting in delays or denial of entry. The new designation adds a compliance obligation for operators trading between East Africa and the US, including vessels calling at Somali ports before proceeding to other destinations. Somalia joins countries including Iran, Yemen, Libya, Sudan and Venezuela on the list. The Coast Guard removed Nigeria from the advisory in August following a reassessment of its port security arrangements. The measure is separate from maritime warnings concerning piracy and attacks on shipping in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. articles.title: Subsea Vessel Market: Shifting Dynamics + Fleet Expansion
articles.summary: We are entering in interesting period in the subsea vessel market, as contract backlog among the EPCs continue to rise to new all-time highs, existing long-term contracts are coming up for renewals, and a wave of newbuilds are closing in on delivery.
articles.body: Subsea Vessel Market: Shifting Dynamics + Fleet Expansion Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Aleksander Gussøy Paulsen , Contributor Aleksander Gussøy Paulsen is a Market Analyst at Fearnley Offshore Supply... October 29, 2026 © NickEyes We are entering in interesting period in the subsea vessel market, as contract backlog among the EPCs continue to rise to new all-time highs, existing long-term contracts are coming up for renewals, and a wave of newbuilds are closing in on delivery. On the top end, the market dynamics are changing as the Tier 1 EPC landscape is consolidating, while the fleet is expected to see a net growth of more than 20% in the coming two years. The still pending merger between Saipem and Subsea 7 is getting closer, with now only the European Commission’s Phase II review outstanding at the time of writing. The European Commissions deadline was first 26th November 2026, then extended by 14 working days to the 16th December. Basis the latest official guiding indicates a close between late 2026 and early 2027 with February mentioned several times, where we can expect the initial period will be focused on post-merger integration and organizational optimization. Once the dust settles, the impact in the vessel market is likely to kick in, which we believe could lead to increased pricing power for the charterer. With the market consolidation among the Tier 1 players, it is likely to see competitors with Tier 2 and 3 EPCI capabilities becoming more relevant among the end-clients, who always seek increased selection and a higher degree of competition. A good example of this is where DOF Subsea and DeepOcean would traditionally sit in the IMR and lighter subsea construction segments, but now might be the time to move towards expanding into field development capabilities. In the field development space today, we expect Ocean Installer to be alternative for E&Ps after building an impressive track record on a variety of projects across mooring, SURF, and decommissioning. Over the summer, they received a contract covering SURF and pre-commission at the Bacalhau field from Equinor in Brazil, with expected offshore operations next year, which marks the company’s first entry to the country. While likely not directly tied to the competitive situation, it is an interesting development showcasing a new market participant in the most active region for floating production capacity in the years to come. Agogo FPSO at Walvis Bay, Namibia © Yinson Production Subsea EPCs Secure New Contracts Across Key Offshore Markets Among the Tier 1 EPCs, the contract intake in August and September have been flattish, yet showcasing intake across familiar regions. Turkish Petroleum awarded Subsea7 an extension covering towing, mooring-line installation and connection work for the Sakarya Phase 3 floating production unit in the Turkish Black Sea, with commissioning activities scheduled for 2028. The award is classified as sizeable, implying a contract value of USD 50 and 150 million. In the US Gulf, LLOG Exploration awarded Subsea7 a contract for the fabrication, transportation and installation of a 29 km steel catenary riser and pipe-in-pipe system, together with umbilical and subsea-controls installation, in approximately 1,300 m water depth. Offshore work is expected to start in 2028 and the value is estimated between USD 50 and 150 million. Saipem, who have been engaged with the current work on the Sakarya Phase 2 project, have now received an award from GOE Petrol Sanayi for an approximately eight-month contract for commissioning services on the Osman Gazi floating production unit, which will serve the gas field in the Turkish Black Sea. In Africa, Saipem and Jan De Nul have formed a consortium and signed an LOI with ExxonMobil Mozambique for the Rovuma LNG Phase 1. The LOI covers preliminary engineering, procurement and technical services covering offshore upstream facilities that will connect 18 subsea wells to the onshore LNG plant through subsea pipelines and manifolds. The initial scope is valued at approximately EUR 11 million and the full EPCI award remains subject to FID and regulatory approvals. Saipem also secured an EPCI contract from Azule Energy for the West Hub Tails project offshore Angola. The scope covers approximately 62 km of subsea flowlines, risers and umbilicals tied back to the Agogo FPSO, located around 180 km offshore in water depths of up to 1,750 metres. The contract is valued at approximately USD 350 million and is expected to run for around 2.5 years. Azule Energy awarded TechnipFMC a contract to design and manufacture flexible flowlines, risers and associated equipment to tie production from the West Hub development back to the Agogo FPSO in Block 15/06, offshore Angola. The award is classified as significant, indicating a contract value of between USD 75 million and USD 250 million. In Malaysia, Petronas awarded TechnipFMC an integrated EPCI contract covering the full subsea scope of the Limbayong deepwater greenfield development. The project will utilise TechnipFMC’s Subsea 2.0 configure-to-order platform, and the award is classified as significant, implying a contract value of between USD 75 million and 250 million. On the vessel chartering side, we have seen a relatively slow end of summer with few high profile new long-term contracts awarded. Reach Subsea recently exercised a one-year option for the “Deep Cygnus” from Havila Subsea & Renewables, which will keep her firm towards March 2028. In the higher end segment, DOF Group has received a letter of intent for a contract valued at between USD 50 million and 100 million that would secure work for one of it’s I-class vessels in the first half of 2028. As such, the contract visibility in the 400-ton segment have improved significantly over the last year. On the corporate side, DeepOcean and TFKable Group plan to establish an integrated EPCI offering for offshore-wind inter-array cables, combining cable manufacturing with survey, engineering, transport, trenching, installation and protection. The multi-year programme includes plans for a dedicated newbuild cable-laying vessel. No investment value nor delivery date was disclosed. Similarly in West Arica, diving specialist Mermaid Maritime and Marine Platforms of Nigeria have formed Mermaid Subsea Services, owned 49% by Mermaid and 51% by Marine Platforms, to pursue subsea work for TotalEnergies and other Nigerian operators while meeting local-content requirements. The venture targets subsea EPCI, ROV support, well services and vessel chartering. In Brazil, Petrobras awarded the 2008-built CSV “Normand Valiant” a two-year contract for accommodation support to production activities on the Brazilian continental shelf. The vessel, equipped with a walk-to-work gangway and capacity for 120 people onboard, is expected to start in the fourth quarter of 2026 almost in direct continuation of its current employment and less its scheduled class renewal. Gross contract value is approximately USD 62 million. Ocean Energy Support Vessel (OESV) for Østensjø Rederi built by GONDAN Shipbuilders © GONDAN Newbuild Wave Puts Pressure on Vessel Charter Rates Many EPCs have been conservative in adding new long-term tonnage in recent months, leading to low volumes of new reported fixtures. Multiple EPCs have optional periods that were excised at lower rates than owners’ current expectations, with several vessels reaching option expiry next year. As the total orderbook across 150 to 400-ton crane vessels now total roughly 35 vessels, we see a market with charterers will have ample choice from existing tonnage and newbuilds. As an example, Østensjø Rederi has now launched the 120-meter Ocean Energy Support Vessel built at Gondan in Spain, with delivery scheduled for late 2027 following outfitting and sea trials. The vessel is designed for a combination of walk-to-work and CSOV support, offshore construction, subsea installation, ROV work, as well as cable laying and repair, with 1,400 m² deck space and accommodation for 173 people onboard. While the contract value has not been publicly disclosed, a European built vessel with this level of specifications comes at a premium. Other owners with uncommitted 250-tonne units scheduled for delivery between Q4 2026 and Q2 2027 include Rem Offshore, Island Offshore and Sea1. Given the current scarcity of active long-term requirements from the major EPCs, we expect owners to show greater commercial flexibility to secure contract coverage ahead of delivery. This trend is already evident in the 150- and 250-tonne segments, where time-charter rates for the latest long-term fixtures have softened from the peaks recorded in 2024 and 2025. We also expect an increasingly notable rate differential between owners capable of delivering integrated scopes, including ROV and engineering services, and those providing vessel capacity alone. These market dynamics could shift relatively quickly in owners’ favour, as only a limited number of long-term requirements would be needed to absorb a meaningful share of the speculative orderbook. Given the record EPC backlog and the underlying pipeline of subsea opportunities, we would not be surprised to see vessel contracting activity increase over the medium term. However, while active requirements remain limited and the fleet continues to expand, we expect near-term upside in charter rates to remain constrained.

articles.title: Egypt’s energy infrastructure grows as two new offshore platforms slide into place
articles.summary: Petroleum Marine Services (PMS) has installed two offshore platforms at North Sinai’s gas field, boosting Egypt's energy infrastructure arsenal.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 29, 2026 · 1 hour ago Egypt’s energy infrastructure grows as two new offshore platforms slide into place Petroleum Marine Services (PMS) has installed two offshore platforms at North Sinai’s gas field, boosting Egypt's energy infrastructure arsenal. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Hoor-1/2 platform installation Source: Petroleum Marine Services (PMS) Egyptian marine and offshore services provider Petroleum Marine Services (PMS) has wrapped up the installation of two platforms as part of Phase Four of a gas field development off the coast of Egypt, paving the way for the fifth phase and supporting efforts to meet the country’s growing domestic gas demand. PMS has completed the installation of two offshore production platforms, Hoor-1/2 and KSE-1 , as part of Phase Four of the development project at the Kamose offshore gas field, operated by North Sinai Petroleum Company (NOSPCO) , in line with the objectives of the Egyptian Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources’ strategy to increase natural gas production. Petroleum Marine Services emphasizes that this installation supports plans to develop natural gas fields and strengthen the country’s offshore petroleum infrastructure. The Hoor-1/2 offshore platform is designed to accommodate two wells, with the first to be drilled as part of the current fourth phase of the project, while the second will be spudded during the upcoming fifth phase. PMS’ scope of work included the installation of two production platforms, each weighing 575 tonnes, with a total weight of 1,150 tonnes. These operations were carried out using the company’s own PMS-12 offshore barge and supporting marine units, in full compliance with the highest quality and safety standards and in accordance with the project’s approved schedule. According to the Egyptian firm, PMS-12 is considered one of the strategic assets in its marine fleet, equipped with the technical capabilities and operational capacity required to install production platforms and lay and deploy subsea pipelines. KSE-1 platform installation; Source: PMS PMS highlighted: “This achievement underscores Petroleum Marine Services’ capabilities in executing complex offshore construction projects, drawing on the expertise of its Egyptian workforce and its advanced marine fleet. “The completion of these works builds on the company’s successful completion of the installation and laying of the project’s three subsea pipelines, each with a diameter of 8 inches, supporting the completion of the offshore infrastructure required for the field’s development.” The company aims to proceed with the subsequent project phases by installing the Snefru offshore production platform, weighing 510 tonnes, followed by the scheduled tie-in and commissioning activities within the project scope. The installation of the two platforms comes after Petroleum Marine Services finished a project in Egypt’s Gulf of Suez, including the installation of an 18-kilometer gas pipeline and upgrades to the asset’s offshore platform at a field operated by Gemsa Petroleum Company (Gempetco). Seaway7's teams installed 95 inter-array cables, totalling more than 240 kilometers of cable loaded, laid and pulled into the foundations at the site. The achievement forms part of Seaway7’s wider scope on East Anglia Three, encompassing the foundations and inter-array cables for the project, and follows the completion of installation of all 95 monopile foundations and transition pieces earlier this year. With cable lay now complete, testing, termination and trenching activities continue as we progress the remaining work towards completion of Seaway7’s full project scope. Wind turbine installation, which started in April, is also under way and is expected to be completed this year, with East Anglia Three scheduled to become fully operational by the end of 2026. articles.summary: Water levels on the Rhine, a critical European inland waterway for freight, rose above 50 centimeters Oct. 26 and are forecast to hover around 70 cm in the next few days, but the rebound in flows is expected to provide only short-term relief to fuel supply chains across the region, according to market participants....
articles.body: Water levels on Rhine rise, but relief forecast to be short-lived in International Shipping News 29/10/2026 Water levels on the Rhine, a critical European inland waterway for freight, rose above 50 centimeters Oct. 26 and are forecast to hover around 70 cm in the next few days, but the rebound in flows is expected to provide only short-term relief to fuel supply chains across the region, according to market participants. Water levels at Kaub, the shallowest part of the Middle Rhine, stood at 56 cm as of late afternoon Oct. 26 and are forecast to exceed 70 cm by the end of the day, then expected to hold around that level for the following three days, according to data from the German water authority WSV. The Rhine water levels exceeded 50 cm on Oct. 26 for the first time since Sept. 4, with levels mostly below 10 cm from Sept. 24 to Oct. 10 and mostly below 20 cm from Oct. 11 to Oct. 22. The recent rise in Rhine water levels has generated renewed market activity, but the improvement is expected to be short-lived, according to a European-based market participant who asked for anonymity because the participant was not authorized to speak publicly. The source said extremely low water levels in recent weeks had forced refiners to rely more heavily on trucks, rail, pipelines, and some coaster movements to transport products, although overall product movements remained slow. A second market participant similarly said the latest rise is unlikely to provide meaningful relief, as the window for barges to pass the Maxau area is expected to be too short to materially ease logistical constraints. Conditions are particularly tight in Switzerland, according to the source, where product inventories are extremely low and market participants are focused on maintaining supplies to retail stations. The Swiss government authorized the release of diesel inventories Oct. 23 to address shortages connected to pipeline delivery delays due to heavy rainfall in southern France. Switzerland also approved the release of jet fuel stocks earlier this month. “Switzerland’s logistical supply has been severely affected for months by the persistent low water levels on the Rhine. If a problem arises with one of the other modes of transport, this can quickly lead to a bottleneck,” the Swiss Federal Office for National Economic Supply said. Germany is comparatively less affected, according to the market participant, because of its larger refining base and less severe isolation from Rhine supply routes, although low water levels continue to restrict river transportation. That said, rail options in Germany remain limited due to the ongoing closure for refurbishment of the right-bank Middle Rhine Line, a key German freight route. The line is expected to stay closed until Dec. 12. “The situation for refiners along the Rhine remains broadly unchanged in October, with the month-to-date average water level at Kaub at around 14 cm. Crude supply remains relatively stable, but the main logistical challenge is clearing refined products amid higher freight costs due to highly limited options,” said Sammir Lesage, analyst at S&P Global Energy CERA. “Those additional costs are likely to be passed through the supply chain, with consumers ultimately bearing much of the burden”, Lesage added. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the ULSD 10 ppm Northwest European Cargo flat price at $1,524.75 mt Oct. 23, while the ULSD 10 ppm Mediterranean Cargo flat price was assessed at $1,518.50 mt. For context, ULSD 10 ppm NWE Cargo September average was $1,503.63 mt and August average was $1,290.63 mt, while the ULSD 10 ppm MED Cargo September average was $1,512.43 and August average was $1,322.56. Freight costs from Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub to Basel, Switzerland, were at €255/mt ($285.27/mt), where they have held since Oct.8, Spotbarge data showed. articles.body: Bahri: Nine-Months 2026 Results With Net Profit Of SAR 9.98 Billion in International Shipping News 29/10/2026 The National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia (Bahri), the Kingdom’s leading shipping and logistics company, announced its financial results for the third quarter and first nine months of 2026, reporting net profit of SAR 5.09 billion for Q3 2026, up 891% year-on-year, while net profit for the first nine months reached SAR 9.98 billion, an increase of 587% compared with the same period last year. Bahri recorded Q3 revenues of SAR 14.83 billion, up 504% year-on-year, while revenues for the first nine months of 2026 reached SAR 26.10 billion, representing growth of 268%. The strong performance was primarily driven by Bahri Oil, which benefited from significantly higher realised VLCC freight rates and increased charter-in activity amid continued regional shipping disruption and strong customer demand. Bahri Chemicals & Products, Integrated Logistics and Dry Bulk also delivered year-on-year revenue growth during the quarter. The results reflect Bahri’s continued ability to adapt to rapidly evolving trade flows and market conditions while maintaining commercial activity through an exceptionally challenging operating environment. During the third quarter, the Company continued to deploy additional chartered capacity where required to meet customer demand, while its diversified businesses responded to changing cargo flows across the region. Bahri also continued to advance its long-term growth and fleet diversification strategy. During Q3 2026, the Company entered the LPG and ammonia shipping segment through the acquisition of three second-hand medium gas carriers. The first vessel was delivered in September, with the remaining two expected in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, respectively. The Company’s owned fleet remained at 107 vessels at end-September 2026, following the addition of the fifth IMO2 MR tanker from its previously announced acquisition programme and the disposal of an older chemical tanker. Bahri also took delivery of two previously ordered offshore support vessels during the quarter. Following the end of Q3, Bahri signed a SAR 1.692 billion agreement with International Maritime Industries (IMI) for the construction of three new VLCCs for delivery between 2029 and 2030, further supporting the Company’s fleet modernisation programme and contributing to the development of domestic shipbuilding capabilities in line with Saudi Vision 2030. Commenting on the results, Eng. Ahmed Ali Al Subaey, Chief Executive Officer of Bahri, said: “Bahri delivered another strong quarter, in an exceptionally complex operating environment, reflecting the resilience of our business model, the strength of our fleet and the discipline with which we continue to execute our strategy. As trade flows shifted and customer requirements evolved, we adapted quickly while maintaining the reliable movement of essential cargo across the Kingdom and global markets. This ability to respond through the cycle is increasingly important in an industry where resilience, scale and flexibility are becoming as critical as capacity itself. Throughout this challenging period, the safety and well-being of our people remained our highest priority. During the quarter, several of our vessels were affected by security incidents, which tragically resulted in the loss of two crew members. We are deeply saddened by their loss and extend our heartfelt condolences to their families and loved ones. These events are a profound reminder of the conditions in which our seafarers operate and reinforce our responsibility to protect our people. I am extremely proud of the professionalism shown by our crews and onshore teams in responding to these incidents and supporting the safe restoration of affected vessels wherever possible. Looking ahead, we are entering the next phase of Bahri’s growth from a position of strength. We are continuing to modernise and diversify our fleet, strengthen our core shipping and logistics businesses and expand selectively into new segments, including gas and ammonia transportation. Our focus remains on disciplined growth that strengthens Bahri’s competitiveness, supports the Kingdom’s expanding trade and maritime ambitions, and creates sustainable long-term value for our shareholders.” Bahri’s strong performance during the first nine months of the year further strengthened its financial position. Net operating cash flow reached SAR 4.07 billion, up 83% year-on-year, while free cash flow reached SAR 2.99 billion, compared with an outflow of SAR 1.31 billion in the prior-year period. Net debt declined to SAR 8.16 billion at end-September 2026, compared with SAR 9.85 billion a year earlier. Combined with stronger earnings, this resulted in the Company’s net debt-to-EBITDA ratio improving to 0.59x, from 2.11x at end-September 2025, providing continued financial flexibility to support Bahri’s long-term growth strategy. During Q3, Bahri also completed a SAR 987 million refinancing facility with BNP Paribas and the National Bank of Greece, marking the Company’s first unsecured international bank financing facility and an important step in further diversification of its funding sources. Operationally, Bahri continued shipping operations amid heightened disruption across the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea. During the first nine months of the year, four owned vessels were impacted by security-related incidents, resulting in the tragic loss of two crew members. Two of the affected vessels have since returned to commercial operations following repairs, while two remain under repair. Bahri maintained its focus on safe and responsible maritime operations, recording no oil spills during Q3 2026. The 12-month rolling Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate for crews serving on Bahri-owned vessels stood at 0.18 injuries per million work hours, compared with 0.23 at end-September 2025. articles.body: ENGINE: Europe & Africa Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 29/10/2026 Northwest Europe Prompt fuel availability is tight in the ARA ports, and buyers are recommended lead times of 5-7 days to get good coverage from suppliers, a trader told ENGINE. B100 demand has picked up in Rotterdam as the biofuel grade trades at a wide discount to LSMGO, the trader said. Rotterdam’s B100 price has fallen by around $182/mt in the past month, to $1,182/mt, according to ENGINE data. That puts it $265/mt below the port’s LSMGO price of $1,447/mt, and the gap has widened by $194/mt in a month. The ARA’s independently held fuel oil stocks have averaged 7% higher in October so far than in September, according to Insights Global data. Stocks have risen 62% since May, when they hit their lowest level in more than a decade. But they are still 9% below February levels, before Israel and the US went to war with Iran. The region’s independent gasoil stocks, which include diesel and heating oil, have gained 6% in October so far compared to September, Insights Global data shows. Fuel availability is stable in Hamburg, with suppliers asking for a notice of five days, a trader told ENGINE. Buyers are advised to allow longer lead times of 10 days for supplies off Denmark’s Skaw and in Sweden’s Gothenburg, a trader said. Mediterranean Prompt bunker fuel availability is tight at the Gibraltar Strait ports, with buyers recommended lead times of 7-10 days to get good coverage from suppliers, a trader told ENGINE. Suppliers in Gibraltar are delivering without delays, port agent MH Bland said. In Algeciras on the other hand, some suppliers are running anywhere between 4-12 hours behind schedule. Suppliers need around a week of notice for deliveries in the Spanish port of Barcelona. Fuel availability is tight in Las Palmas, with buyers advised lead times of 7-8 days to get deliveries, a trader said. Bunker availability is tight in Togo’s Lome, and buyers are recommended lead times of 5-7 days for VLSFO and LSMGO supplies, a trader told ENGINE. VLSFO availability is tight in Nigeria’s Lagos anchorage, and buyers are recommended lead times of 10-12 days, a local supplier told ENGINE. VLSFO is unavailable in Angola’s Luanda, while LSMGO deliveries need lead times of 5-7 days, a supplier told ENGINE. Fuel supplies off Namibia’s Walvis Bay are tight for prompt dates. Buyers are advised 5-7 days of lead time for VLSFO and LSMGO deliveries, a trader told ENGINE. Fuel availability is tight in the South African ports of Durban and Cape Town. Buyers are recommended 10-15 days of notice to secure deliveries, a trader told ENGINE. Fuel availability is very tight in Port Louis. Buyers are recommended to book 10-14 days in advance to secure supplies, a trader said. VLSFO supply has restarted in Djibouti’s ports after a disruption, and both VLSFO and LSMGO can be delivered on a prompt basis to vessels, a local supplier told ENGINE. articles.body: Valenciaport makes progress on the construction of the new substation to strengthen the electrification of the Port of València in Port News 29/10/2026 The Port Authority of València (PAV) has launched the tender process for the construction of a new electrical substation at the Port of València, an infrastructure project that will enable Valenciaport to double the port’s electricity supply capacity. This step follows authorisation by the Spanish Council of Ministers. The project is expected to take 20 months to complete and will involve an estimated investment of €18.7 million. It will strengthen the electricity supply to meet the anticipated increase in energy demand over the coming years, driven both by the activities of terminals, companies and concession holders, and by the port’s electrification process. The investment is supported by the European Commission through the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). ST2 will have a shared available capacity with ST1, ranging from a maximum of 90 megawatts (MW) to a minimum of 40 megawatts (MW), depending on whether it is supplied through one of the two ST-Aqua lines or one of the two ST-Punta lines, respectively. Its commissioning will enable the facility to meet the growing energy demand of cargo terminals, logistics infrastructure and new Onshore Power Supply (OPS) systems for vessels. This will enable the interconnection of the Port Authority of Valencia (APV) power supply network in the northern area of the port with the high-voltage distribution network. The existence of two independently operated substations connected through separate incoming connections will enable a high-availability power supply configuration and strengthen the energy resilience of the port facility. In this way, in the event of network incidents, maintenance works or exceptional periods of high demand, the port’s internal grid will be able to draw power from the second substation without the need to interrupt terminal operations. This capability is particularly important for ensuring the continuity of critical operations, such as crane operations and the power supply to refrigerated containers (reefers). The new facility has been designed with sustainability and landscape integration criteria and will incorporate GIS technology, which allows high-voltage equipment to be housed within a sealed enclosure, reducing the risk of leaks of polluting fluids into the soil or sea. Infrastructure for port electrification The second substation will not only strengthen the quality and continuity of the Port of Valencia’s internal power grid, but will also provide the capacity needed to advance the electrification of port operations and the deployment of new energy infrastructure. These include Onshore Power Supply (OPS) systems, which allow berthed vessels to connect to the shore-side electricity grid and switch off their auxiliary engines while in port. This helps reduce emissions associated with these engines, as well as the noise impact of port activities on the surrounding area. Steady high-volume operations at Shenzhen Port are underpinned by forward-looking smart port infrastructure. Its Yantian East Terminal is equipped with China’s largest automated twin-lift quay cranes, which can handle 32,000-TEU ultra-large container vessels, 33 percent bigger than the world’s largest ships currently in service. Mawan Smart Port, the country’s first smart terminal upgraded from a conventional container dock and Shenzhen’s first pilot project under China’s initiative to become a transport powerhouse, uses an independently developed terminal operating system alongside a 5G autonomous truck management platform to automate core terminal workflows. Shore power consumption in the first nine months reached 47.7 million kWh, up 34 percent year-on-year. South China’s most powerful fully electric smart tugboat is now in service. articles.title: Dry Bulk Market: Escalating Attacks Heighten Uncertainty
articles.summary: "Geopolitical disruptions continue to cloud the dry bulk market outlook. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz remains the largest source of uncertainty, while attacks on ships and port infrastructure in the Black Sea have added another layer of risk…
articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Escalating Attacks Heighten Uncertainty Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Image courtesy BIMCO "Geopolitical disruptions continue to cloud the dry bulk market outlook. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz remains the largest source of uncertainty, while attacks on ships and port infrastructure in the Black Sea have added another layer of risk,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. Typically, around 4% of dry bulk demand sails via the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative routes have softened the impact of the disruption but have been unable to replace pre-war volumes. The disruption has also tightened energy and fertiliser supplies, weighing on global economic growth and raising concerns over food security. Given the uncertainty, BIMCO presents two forecast scenarios. The “SoH closed” scenario assumes that the strait remains effectively closed throughout 2027 and 2028, while the “SoH open” scenario assumes that ships can freely transit the strait from 2027 onwards. “We expect the dry bulk supply/demand balance to gradually weaken in 2027 and 2028, although from a high baseline. Cargo volume growth is expected to be limited, while ship deliveries accelerate, particularly in the capesize segment,” says Gouveia. In 2027, ship demand is forecast to grow 0.5-2.5% if the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed, compared with supply growth of 3-4%. If the strait reopens, both demand and supply growth are expected to be 1 percentage point higher. In this scenario, demand would grow faster for commodities other than coal supported by improved economic conditions and stronger import demand from countries in the Persian Gulf. However, the fleet currently trapped in the Gulf would begin operating as normal and sailing speeds could remain slightly higher than in our other scenario, increasing supply. In 2028, ship demand is forecast to grow 0.5-2.5% in both scenarios, while supply is expected to grow 3-4%. Cargo volume growth is expected to remain limited as coal shipments decline, while the return of bulkers to the Panama Canal could weigh on average sailing distance growth. On the supply side, rising ship deliveries are expected to support strong fleet growth, even as ship recycling increases. Lastly, average sailing speeds are expected to decrease slightly as market conditions soften. “Disruptions to Black Sea shipping pose an additional downside risk to the market outlook. The forecast assumes that Russian and Ukrainian grain volumes unable to be shipped in 2026 are instead exported in 2027. If they remain unavailable, dry bulk cargo growth could be up to 0.5 percentage points weaker in 2027 and grain shipment growth up to 4 percentage points weaker,” says Gouveia.

articles.title: Electric Container Barge Launched in Vietnam
articles.summary: CMA CGM, Nike and Vietnamese port operator Gemadept have launched a fully electric inland container barge service connecting Ho Chi Minh City with the Gemalink deep-sea terminal at Cai Mep, combining battery propulsion, dedicated charging infrastructure…
articles.body: Electric Container Barge Launched in Vietnam Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Image courtresy CMA CGM CMA CGM, Nike and Vietnamese port operator Gemadept have launched a fully electric inland container barge service connecting Ho Chi Minh City with the Gemalink deep-sea terminal at Cai Mep, combining battery propulsion, dedicated charging infrastructure and renewable electricity. The barge will transport Nike cargo between an inland drop-off location in Ho Chi Minh City, formerly part of Binh Duong province, and Gemalink over a 180-km round trip. Designed to handle more than 50,000 TEU annually , the vessel offers an alternative to road transportation while producing no direct greenhouse gas emissions during operation. According to the partners, the service is expected to avoid approximately 778 metric tons of CO2 emissions annually. Developed by CMA CGM's New Build and R&D teams, the barge incorporates battery technology supplied by CATL. Its batteries can be recharged in approximately four hours using certified renewable electricity. The charging infrastructure at Gemalink is supported by a dedicated solar farm developed at the terminal, integrating renewable power generation with inland waterway transportation. The project is intended to reduce emissions associated with Nike's cargo movements while demonstrating how electric propulsion can be incorporated into existing port and logistics networks. "Decarbonizing global supply chains requires moving beyond ambition to deliver concrete, scalable solutions," said Christine Cabau, Executive Vice President Assets and Operations at CMA CGM. The companies are evaluating opportunities to replicate the arrangement in other markets and adapt it to additional customer supply chains. For CMA CGM, the initiative expands its intermodal logistics activities in Vietnam, where the company operates 29 weekly mainline shipping services calling at seven ports. The project also highlights the potential for battery-powered vessels on established inland routes where predictable voyage distances and access to shoreside charging can support commercial operations without onboard combustion engines.

articles.title: Three Bodies Found in Sunken Borr Drilling Rig Off Gabon, Two Still Missing
articles.summary: Three bodies have been located inside the wreck of Borr Drilling's Prospector 5 jack-up rig, which sank offshore Gabon on October 24, with search and rescue operations continuing for two people still missing, according to the Gabonese Navy.The…
articles.body: Three Bodies Found in Sunken Borr Drilling Rig Off Gabon, Two Still Missing Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Prospector 5 jack-up rig (Credit: Screenshot/Youtube) Three bodies have been located inside the wreck of Borr Drilling's Prospector 5 jack-up rig, which sank offshore Gabon on October 24, with search and rescue operations continuing for two people still missing, according to the Gabonese Navy. The bodies were discovered during underwater inspections using a remotely operated vehicle (ROV), Vice-Admiral Charles Hubert Bekale-Meyong, chief of staff of the Gabonese Navy and commander of the search-and-rescue operation, confirmed in an October 28 statement. The images obtained did not allow the bodies to be identified, while technical teams were preparing operations to recover them. “Of the five people reported missing, three bodies were located on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, inside the still-submerged wreck,” said Vice-Admiral Charles Hubert Bekale-Meyong. Of the 115 people on board when the rig sank, 110 were rescued. A judicial investigation into the incident was opened on October 25. The Prospector 5, owned and operated by Borr Drilling, sank after experiencing a punch-through event during preload operations, causing it to lose stability while preparing for a drilling campaign on BW Energy's Dussafu Marine licence. The incident occurred at approximately 8:37 pm local time on October 24 during jacking operations ahead of the MaBoMo Phase 2 drilling campaign. Built in 2014, the Prospector 5 is an F&G JU-2000E jack-up drilling rig with a maximum operating water depth of 400 feet and a maximum drilling depth of 35,000 feet. BW Energy Flags Drilling Delays, MaBoMo Production Resumes BW Energy confirmed on October 29 that the incident would delay first oil from the MaBoMo Phase 2 campaign, with the company assessing its impact on the drilling schedule and 2027 production outlook. The remaining Phase 2 wells will be considered within the wider Dussafu drilling program, while BW Energy maintains its target of producing more than 100,000 barrels of oil per day in 2028. Production at the MaBoMo facility, which was shut down in accordance with standard procedures during drilling preparations, has resumed, with no damage to BW Energy's facilities identified. "Production from MaBoMo has resumed, and the two discoveries made earlier in the campaign add to the resources we plan to develop in Phase 2. The incident affects the timing of those barrels rather than the resources themselves," said Carl Arnet, CEO of BW Energy. The company continues to support the search and rescue operations in coordination with Gabonese authorities and Borr Drilling. articles.body: Europe Offshore Aker Solutions braces for more job cuts Bojan Lepic October 29, 2026 0 183 1 minute read Aker Solutions Aker Solutions Norwegian offshore engineering group Aker Solutions is preparing for another round of workforce reductions as a sharp decline in activity following the completion of major oil and gas projects threatens hundreds more jobs. Chief financial officer Idar Eikrem told analysts during the company’s third-quarter results presentation that the contractor should expect further staffing adjustments as it prepares for significantly lower revenues in 2027. Eikrem pointed to the reduction of between 200 and 300 positions at the company’s Verdal yard late last year, adding that similar measures should be expected going forward. Chief executive Paal Eikeseth said the company was reshaping its operations as the market shifts away from major offshore developments towards smaller subsea tieback projects. The company will provide further details on the planned adjustments, including numbers, before the end of the year. The warning follows a restructuring programme announced in January, when Aker Solutions said more than 500 permanent positions could be affected, including around 300 at Verdal. The company expects revenue to fall to between NOK35bn ($3.78bn) and NOK40bn ($4.32bn) in 2027, compared with its forecast of NOK53bn ($5.73bn) to NOK55bn ($5.95bn) for this year. The anticipated downturn comes as major projects move towards completion. In the third quarter, Aker Solutions shipped the Valhall PWP and Hugin B topsides for Aker BP, while the remaining Hugin A topsides are expected to leave the yard in winter. Norwegian media have also reported growing concerns about employment at the company’s Stord facility, where union representatives hope to avoid layoffs by transferring workers to offshore assignments and projects elsewhere in Norway. The unions have pointed to Equinor’s planned Wisting development in the Barents Sea as potentially crucial for securing future work. Despite the looming downturn, Aker Solutions reported third-quarter revenue of NOK13.5bn ($1.46bn) and underlying EBITDA of NOK1.3bn ($141m). New orders totalled NOK5.4bn ($584m), leaving the company with a backlog of NOK69.3bn ($7.49bn) at the end of September. articles.title: Built for the Dead Sea: Purpose-Built Workboat for Extreme Ops
articles.summary: ECTMarine delivered a purpose-built workboat to Arab Potash Company (APC) in Jordan following successful site acceptance testing (SAT).The SAT of the Custom Workboat 104 was completed last week on APC's brine evaporation ponds at the Dead Sea.
articles.body: Built for the Dead Sea: Purpose-Built Workboat for Extreme Ops Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 29, 2026 Image courtesy ECTMarine Image courtesy ECTMarine ECTMarine delivered a purpose-built workboat to Arab Potash Company (APC) in Jordan following successful site acceptance testing (SAT). The SAT of the Custom Workboat 104 was completed last week on APC's brine evaporation ponds at the Dead Sea. APC was represented on site by its main contractor, Alghanem. Designed and built in the Netherlands, the workboat was tailored to the conditions at the Dead Sea, where the dense, highly saline brine and the site’s location around 400 metres below sea level posed specific challenges. The Custom Workboat 104 features a forward wheelhouse, an open working deck and a knuckle-boom deck crane. ECTMarine designed the vessel around APC’s operational requirements, with a hull and deck layout suitable for road transport on a standard flat rack. “The Dead Sea is not a normal place to operate a boat. The brine is extremely dense and corrosive, the site is remote, and the vessel has to be moved by road and lifted in by crane. We needed a workboat built around those conditions and around the tasks APC performs on the ponds. ECTMarine took the time to understand that before they started designing,” said Abdallah Ghammaz, Project Manager at Alghanem. The vessel completed its factory acceptance test (FAT) in the Netherlands in summer 2026. During a two-day program, a delegation representing the buyer witnessed a sea trial and demonstrations of the vessel’s systems, operating modes and configurations. Adjustments agreed during the FAT were completed before shipment. The workboat was shipped to Jordan on a flat rack and trucked along the dykes of APC's evaporation ponds to the launch point. There, a mobile crane with a double spreader-bar rig lifted it from the trailer into the brine. ECTMarine, Alghanem and APC jointly conducted the SAT, testing the vessel’s propulsion, deck crane and onboard systems under operating conditions. Following successful completion of the tests, the workboat is ready to enter service. “The SAT confirmed that the vessel does what it was designed to do, in the real conditions on the ponds. Seeing it float in the brine for the first time and then pass every test was a proud moment for everyone involved. The workboat will now go into daily service for APC, and we look forward to seeing it at work,” added Ghammaz. Image courtesy ECTMarine

articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: Union approves LA/Long Beach port strike; container rates still under pressure
articles.summary: The container carrier march back through the Red Sea continues, with Alphaliner estimating nearly two-thirds of total Asia – Europe capacity is now restored. Especially of note is Israeli carrier ZIM’s announcement that it has resumed taking the Red Sea route for its joint Asia – US East Coast service with MSC, as...
articles.body: The container carrier march back through the Red Sea continues, with Alphaliner estimating nearly two-thirds of total Asia – Europe capacity is now restored. Especially of note is Israeli carrier ZIM’s announcement that it has resumed taking the Red Sea route for its joint Asia – US East Coast service with MSC, as the Houthis declared the Bab el-Mandeb Strait closed to Israel-linked vessels as recently as August. Another typhoon rumbled through the Far East starting last week. Typhoon Champi closed container ports and airports in Taiwan on Friday, and threatened but mostly spared operations at East China ports before weakening as it continued on toward Japan. The major Chinese container hubs continue their recovery from previous storm disruptions over the summer though most are still not completely back to normal. Congestion has been one factor keeping some pressure on container rates even as demand eases post peak season. Some vessel bunching from ships now taking the shorter Red Sea route and arriving ahead of schedule may be slowing the recovery. Though demand is cool on Asia – Europe lanes carriers are scheduling rate increases for November, with prices already trending up since mid-month as congestion and blanked sailings assist carrier attempts at rate bumps for now. Asia – N. Europe prices climbed 3% to $3,551/FEU last week and rates to the Mediterranean increased 8% to $4,252/FEU. Nonetheless, some forwarders are already reporting carrier discounts and don’t expect additional increases to take. Despite expectations that transpacific prices would cool post-Golden Week, rates climbed last week, increasing 3% to $8,368/FEU to the West Coast and 9% to a new high for the year of $10,565/FEU to the East Coast. Daily prices to the East Coast have receded so far this week but are still up about $200/FEU compared to last week. Some forwarders however report signs of cooling demand and space becoming more available, and still expect a seasonal easing in rates. A local watchmen’s union at the ports of LA and Long Beach voted to authorize a strike, which could be called as soon as November 1st. Though it only represents about 2% of the workforce, the union provides security for a large share of terminals so a strike could have an outsized impact on operations. Labor disruptions would come on top of reports of existing delays for containers moving by rail. The White House extended its trade truce with China in late September, pushing off the expiration date of the status quo for tariffs and other elements of the deal to early January. Though most in the industry assumed that US port call fees on China-linked vessels – also set for November 10th – would also be deferred, the fees are officially still on the books. Last week though the US Trade Representative released a request for comments regarding postponing the port call fees until January as well, suggesting that this policy will also be pushed off. The USTR also recently said that it should complete its Section 301 investigations into excess manufacturing capacity by China and fifteen other countries by the end of the year, despite earlier reports that the studies were ready ahead of the September Trump-Xi meeting. Current tariff levels on several countries including China are actually below the negotiated levels that will expire in January since duties introduced after the Supreme Court invalidated IEEPA-based tariffs did not reach IEEPA levels for all trading partners. The excess capacity investigations are expected to recommend tariffs that would restore duties to IEEPA levels for China and others. If the investigation is wrapped up by the end of the year, it could still take another couple months – to allow the required comments and hearing period – until the administration could use the findings to introduce tariffs. Air cargo rates out of China climbed last week by 4% to $7.13/kg to N. America and 12% to $4.35/kg to Europe as peak season looks to be underway. Daily rates so far this week show additional significant gains to N. America and a sharp increase in South East Asia – US prices, as seasonal demand stacks on top of already strong data center-driven volumes. Judah Levine, Head of Research, Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

articles.body: Asia Containers India greenlights $1bn drive to break China’s container manufacturing dominance Sam Chambers October 29, 2026 0 369 1 minute read LR LR India has approved a INR100bn ($1.05bn) programme to massively expand domestic shipping container manufacturing, targeting a tenfold increase in annual capacity as New Delhi seeks to challenge China’s near-monopoly over the industry. The country’s cabinet approved the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme yesterday, turning a proposal announced in February’s national budget into a 13-year industrial development programme. The initiative aims to increase India’s annual container manufacturing capacity from approximately 70,000 teu today to 750,000 teu, potentially establishing the country as a significant international supplier of shipping containers. Chinese manufacturers currently account for more than 95% of global dry freight container production and virtually the entire refrigerated container market. India hopes to erode that dominance through a combination of production subsidies, subsidised financing and investment in manufacturing infrastructure. The programme includes INR88.91bn in financial assistance for containers manufactured to international standards, alongside INR8.59bn in support for financing new factories and expanding existing production facilities. Manufacturers will be eligible for a 3% annual interest subsidy on qualifying loans. Additional funding will support testing and certification facilities, while manufacturers establishing operations at major ports will receive preferential land leasing arrangements. The government is targeting new factories with annual capacity of at least 100,000 teu, while existing manufacturers must expand capacity by at least 25,000 teu to qualify for financing support. Domestic content requirements will progressively increase from 70% to 90%. The programme runs from the 2027-28 financial year through to 2039-40, allowing three years for establishing facilities followed by ten years of production support. The initiative also complements India’s plans to establish Bharat Container Shipping Line, a state-backed carrier being developed by Shipping Corporation of India, CONCOR and several other government-controlled maritime organisations. articles.title: What the IMO should learn from Brazil’s elections ahead of its historic decision
articles.summary: Elissama Menezes, a Brazilian co-director of Equal Routes, a nonprofit working on shipping decarbonisation, writes for Splash today. Brazil’s presidential elections show that one should never discount the underdog. The same lesson could be applied to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate negotiations,...
articles.body: Contributions Environment Regulatory What the IMO should learn from Brazil’s elections ahead of its historic decision Splash October 29, 2026 0 115 3 minutes read IMO IMO Elissama Menezes, a Brazilian co-director of Equal Routes, a nonprofit working on shipping decarbonisation, writes for Splash today. Brazil’s presidential elections show that one should never discount the underdog. The same lesson could be applied to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate negotiations, which are resuming in London just next month. Last Sunday, millions of Brazilians elected a candidate who finished second in the first round and made him president in the runoff. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured his fourth term with 51.76% of the vote, against all the odds. The parallels with global shipping are hard to miss. Washington made little secret of which presidential candidate it preferred in Brazil, and at the IMO its position is no less clear. The US administration rejects the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF), a historic agreement to tackle shipping emissions through carbon intensity targets and carbon pricing. The NZF is a hard-fought compromise that was backed by the vast majority of IMO member states when it was reached in April 2025. When this flagship climate policy was set to be adopted, just over a year ago, the US deployed “bully-boy” tactics to narrowly pass a motion to delay the vote by one year. But Brazil presidential elections have now shown that people want climate action, a central issue in the election campaigns. Lula’s victory gives him another four years to pursue his pledge to end deforestation by 2030, following reductions in forest loss during his current term. It also preserves his mandate to continue Brazil’s international climate diplomacy following its hosting of COP30 in Belém in 2025. And this brings us again back to the IMO, where Brazil is an influential player. Brazil is one of the main architects of the NZF, and its policy architecture carries Brazil’s fingerprints. Until Sunday, sceptics could argue that the government behind that work might not last and that the future of the NZF becomes even more uncertain. That argument is gone. Lula’s victory is a re-legitimisation of Brazil’s role at the IMO and gives it a fresh mandate to get the NZF agreement over the finishing line this year. The deeper lesson is about sovereignty. Brazilians were told, in many ways, that their future depended on staying in Washington’s good graces. They rejected that and clearly preferred a leader who stands up to “bullies”. IMO countries in a way face the same choice as average Brazilians. And every month without strong global rules has a price. Fuel producers and shipowners need a stable signal to invest in e-fuels, wind-assisted propulsion and other zero-emission options. Without it, projects stall and first movers are punished. Delay prolongs uncertainty just as the sector must cut short-lived climate pollutants such as methane, which slips from the growing LNG-fuelled fleet. It also postpones the revenue mechanisms meant to make this transition fair for the countries least responsible for the problem. Europe’s own rules, the EU ETS for shipping and FuelEU Maritime, help fill the regulatory vacuum, but they cannot do the job alone. FuelEU’s steepest cuts do not arrive until the 2040s, leaving room for business as usual in the near term. Its emission factors must also capture methane accurately. Until a global rule exists, Europe should keep strengthening its regime, but a regional patchwork is no substitute for a global standard. That is why the EU, more than anyone, should take heart from Brazil. Europe helped secure the NZF agreement last year, yet some of its member states abstained when the pressure came last October. The bloc should arrive in London united behind the framework it helped build. And so should the rest of the world, united in support of what they agreed on a year ago. Brazilians did not wait for anyone’s permission to choose their future and neither should the IMO. articles.body: Costamare reported adjusted net income of $89.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with $98 million in the same period last year. The company also reported approximately $6 billion in contracted containership revenues, supported by long-term charter agreements. Adjusted earnings from continuing operations reached $0.74 per share, down from $0.81 a year earlier. Meanwhile, net income from continuing operations available to common stockholders stood at $88.5 million, compared with $92.6 million in the third quarter of 2025. Voyage revenue declined by 1.8% to $212.1 million, from $215.9 million a year earlier. Costamare attributed the decrease mainly to lower charter rates for certain vessels and additional off-hire days, primarily linked to scheduled dry-dockings. Despite the decline in quarterly earnings, the company’s liquidity reached $733.1 million at the end of September 2026. Charter coverage and fleet investment Costamare has secured employment for 100% of its containership fleet capacity in 2026 and 99% in 2027. These figures are calculated on a TEU basis and reflect the company’s charter position as of 27 October. Total contracted revenues reached approximately $6 billion, with a TEU-weighted charter duration of 5.8 years. The backlog includes contracts associated with 22 newbuild containerships and two secondhand vessels that the company has agreed to acquire. Costamare currently has 69 containerships in the water, with a combined capacity of approximately 520,000 TEUs. Its 22 vessels under construction and two planned secondhand acquisitions represent an additional 152,600 TEUs. The company also advanced its refinancing programme during the quarter. Since the end of June, Costamare has completed previously announced financing agreements and drawn $1.3 billion to refinance debt across 39 vessels. In addition, the company signed a $92 million loan agreement with an Asian bank for two vessels. It expects to draw the funds during the fourth quarter of 2026. According to Costamare, the new financing arrangements will reduce interest costs and extend debt maturities. Gregory Zikos, Chief Financial Officer of Costamare, said the refinancing programme would leave the company without debt maturities until 2030. Zikos also commented on the containership charter market. He noted that idle vessel capacity remained below 1%, reflecting strong fleet employment. “The fast-rising number of shipping services returning to the Suez Canal has not yet affected market fundamentals,” said Zikos. Beyond its containership operations, Costamare continues to develop Neptune Maritime Leasing, in which it holds a controlling interest. The platform has 47 shipping assets funded or under commitment, with total investments and commitments exceeding $650 million. The latest results follow Costamare’s third-quarter 2025 financial report, when the company reported $2.6 billion in contracted containership revenues. Costamare also declared a quarterly common stock dividend of $0.125 per share, payable on 5 November 2026.

articles.body: CMA CGM has launched its first dedicated block train service between the Port of Mombasa and the Nairobi-Embakasi Inland Container Depot (ICD) in Kenya. The new connection aims to strengthen container transport between the country’s main seaport and its inland markets. The service began on 28 October 2026 and operates with 54 wagons, offering capacity for 108 TEUs per train. Initially, CMA CGM will run one train per week, carrying imported containers from Mombasa to Nairobi. The shipping company developed the service in partnership with the Kenya Ports Authority (KPA) and Kenya Railways Corporation (KRC). The initiative forms part of CMA CGM’s efforts to expand its inland logistics network across East Africa. Strengthening inland container connections The new rail service connects Mombasa with Nairobi’s Embakasi ICD, supporting the movement of imported goods into Kenya’s main inland economic centre. CMA CGM will initially focus on import shipments while assessing customer demand. Depending on market requirements, the company may increase train frequency and introduce a return service from Nairobi to Mombasa. By linking rail transport with its maritime operations, CMA CGM aims to offer customers more integrated logistics services. The connection also supports cooperation between shipping lines, port operators and railway authorities. “Today’s launch is an important milestone for CMA CGM in Kenya. Our ambition is to strengthen connectivity between the sea, the port and inland economies,” said Naveen Prabhu, Deputy Regional Director for East Africa at CMA CGM. He also highlighted the importance of cooperation with the Kenyan government, KPA, KRC and customers in developing the service. Mohamed Daghar, Principal Secretary for Transport at Kenya’s Ministry of Roads and Transport, said stronger connections between Mombasa and inland economic centres are important for the country’s logistics network. “Partnerships between maritime and rail transport stakeholders help connect infrastructure, businesses and markets,” said Daghar. The new service adds to CMA CGM’s existing inland logistics activities in Kenya, including its Kilima service. The company is also working with Bandari Maritime Academy to support training for maritime and logistics professionals. The launch strengthens CMA CGM’s transport offering in East Africa by connecting its maritime services with dedicated rail capacity. Further expansion will depend on demand and the performance of the initial weekly service.

articles.title: North Sea gas discovery twice as big after appraisal success with tie-back on the table
articles.summary: Appraisal activities have doubled a North Sea gas discovery’s estimate, with a potential tie-back to existing infrastructure being contemplated.
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 29, 2026 · 4 hours ago North Sea gas discovery twice as big after appraisal success with tie-back on the table Appraisal activities have doubled a North Sea gas discovery’s estimate, with a potential tie-back to existing infrastructure being contemplated. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Kvitebjørn platform in the North Sea Credit: Torstein Lund Eik/Equinor Norway’s state-owned energy giant Equinor and its partners have achieved a twofold increase of their initial estimate for a gas discovery in the North Sea, revealing recoverable gas and condensate volumes of up to 180 million barrels of oil equivalent (boe) following the drilling of an appraisal well. As a result, the partners are now eyeing a potential subsea tie-back to existing infrastructure to bring more gas to the European market. The Norwegian Offshore Directorate has disclosed that Equinor, together with its partners, Orlen Upstream Norway , DNO Norge , and Wellesley Petroleum , drilled the 35/7-2 appraisal well about 35 kilometers northeast of the Kvitebjørn field on the 35/7-1 well, also known as the Afrodite discovery, which was made in 2008. The well 35/7-2, which confirmed the gas and condensate discovery, was the second well drilled in production license 293, awarded in 2003 (North Sea Awards 2002). Equinor’s partner, Wellesley, is the operator of the well 35/7-2, which was drilled by the Deepsea Yantai rig. The objective of 35/7-2 was to delineate the Afrodite discovery, leading the partners to encounter a 69-meter gas/condensate column in the Tarbert Formation and the upper part of the Ness Formation with reservoir rocks of poor quality. The gas/water contact was not made. A 4-meter gas/condensate column was found in the lower part of the Ness Formation, with reservoir rocks of poor quality and no gas/water contact. The well encountered reservoir rocks with poor reservoir properties in the Etive Formation. This reservoir was aquiferous. Extensive volumes of data were collected in the well, as the use of new technology in the data acquisition provided essential information for developing the reservoir, which yielded beneficial learning for use in other tight reservoirs. The well was drilled to a vertical depth of 4,667 meters below sea level in the Drake Formation, part of the Dunlin Group from the Middle Jurassic. The water depth at the site is 376 meters, and the well is currently being permanently plugged and abandoned. Preliminary calculations show that the discovery is now between 12 and 29 million standard cubic meters of recoverable oil equivalent, which corresponds to between 77 and 180 million barrels of oil equivalent . The licensees will assess whether it is possible to develop Afrodite via existing infrastructure in the area, where Kvitebjørn is one possible option. According to Equinor, the new appraisal well shows that the recoverable gas volumes may be more than twice as large as previously estimated, with total volumes in the reservoir about three times as large, but the reservoir properties mean that only parts of the resources can be recovered. "To find such large gas volumes in a mature area on the Norwegian Continental Shelf is very good. We have long had faith in the Afrodite discovery, and this appraisal well has uncovered volumes far above expectations.” Kjetil Hove · Equinor's Executive Vice President for Exploration & Production Norway The reservoir has relatively low permeability, which means that the gas flows slowly through the reservoir rock and makes the resources difficult to recover, so the results from the appraisal well will now be analyzed further. Equinor considers the discovery to be commercially viable and will continue to work on the possibility of a subsea development tied back to the Kvitebjørn platform so that the gas could be sent via existing infrastructure to the Kollsnes processing plant in Øygarden and on to the European market. " We are investing aggressively in exploration on the Norwegian continental shelf. Equinor strongly believes that there is still more to be discovered and is working purposefully to increase the likelihood of new and larger discoveries. The results at Afrodite show the potential that still exists in mature areas. At the same time, new discoveries in new exploration areas will be crucial for maintaining production from the Norwegian continental shelf and deliveries of energy to Europe. " — Hove highlighted. articles.summary: The UK's National Grid is investing up to £400 million (around €478 million) in the first cross-border electricity link between the UK and...
articles.body: Interconnectors October 29, 2026 · 5 hours ago Huge investment to keep first UK-France interconnector running until at least 2050 NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email National Grid The UK's National Grid is investing up to £400 million (around €478 million) in the first cross-border electricity link between the UK and France, extending the operation of the interconnector commissioned in 1986 until at least 2050. The investment, announced as the Interconnexion France-Angleterre (IFA) project marks 40 years of operation, is part of National Grid’s wider plans to invest at least £70 billion across the group until March 2031. IFA, jointly owned by the National Grid and French transmission system operator (TSO) Réseau de Transport d’Electricité (RTE), was the first modern electricity interconnector linking Great Britain with continental Europe and the second subsea high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cable link in the world when it began operating in 1986. With its 2 GW, the interconnector is still Great Britain’s largest subsea connection by capacity and can carry enough electricity to power approximately three million British homes annually. Since 1986, net imports have totalled an estimated 409TWh, said to be considerably more than a full year of Britain's electricity demand. Although electricity has historically flowed mainly to Great Britain, IFA also supports flows in the opposite direction when market conditions dictate. By extending IFA’s operation to 2050, the investment will support the continued two-way flow of electricity between the two countries, strengthening energy security and delivering value for consumers on both sides. According to the National Grid, the program will include upgrades to essential technical equipment, buildings and facilities at the interconnector site. "For 40 years, our IFA interconnector has been sharing secure and affordable electricity between Great Britain and France. That has delivered benefits for UK consumers and since 2020, IFA has made payments to UK consumers of nearly £300 million," said Rebecca Sedler , President of NGV UK, National Grid. "I’m proud to announce this new investment which will extend the operation of IFA to meet the next phase of electricity demand, from AI to electric vehicles. Our ability to connect both nations will benefit consumers and the energy systems on both sides of the channel." The IFA electrical interconnector is approximately 70 kilometers long, with 45 kilometers being subsea. Besides it, there are two other interconnectors in service that are connecting the two countries, including the 1 GW IFA2, commissioned in January 2021, and the 1 GW ElecLink, commissioned in May 2022.
